name: Jamal Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and won't be traced back to you. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. Confidential is good, because some of what I think about my clients isn't for their ears.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior designer at a six-person agency down by the harbour, and most of what we do is packaging. Jam jar labels, cheese wrappers, beer cans for a little brewery up the hill. My day is half design and half arguing with dielines, which are the flat cut-out shapes a box gets folded from, because one millimetre out and ten thousand labels go in the bin. I love holding a finished can in my hand in a shop. I don't love that I earn about two-thirds of what a city designer does and share a flat with my cousin Idris because I can't afford one alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the tools are handy for mock-ups and rubbish at the real job. I'd probably post a photo of a misprinted can from an AI dieline and make a joke of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm still on the same pay, in the same flat, with about two weeks of money in the bank. My clients are tiny food businesses and half of them are one bad summer from closing. If the cheese farm goes under, our agency loses a fifth of its work, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the image tool for quick mock-ups, maybe an hour saved a week, and that's it. I'd ask for a pay review in January and point at the brewery account I brought in. And I'd try to build a two-month buffer, which at my wages means about a year of being boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little flat, because the big change everyone promised turns out to be the same old squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the same old squeeze, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent up eight percent this year, wages up nothing. Idris and I split everything to the penny on a spreadsheet stuck to the fridge. Same old squeeze means my rent goes up every year and my pay stays exactly where it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which client would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cheese farm on the coast road. The owner, Maeve, rings me personally about every label, and her sales are down since the supermarket stopped stocking her. If her farm closes, I lose the client I like most and the agency loses a big monthly bill.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy for mock-ups** and useless for real packaging.
I'd post a **misprinted can** as a joke about the hype.
think: My **same pay** and two weeks of savings matter more than the tech news.
A **struggling client** closing would hurt the agency more than AI would.
do: Keep using the image tool for **mock-ups**, saving about an hour a week.
Ask for a **pay review** in January, citing the brewery account.
Build a **two-month buffer** over about a year.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but flat that the big change is the same old squeeze.
S0.quote: Same old squeeze means my rent goes up every year and my pay stays exactly where it was.
fieldNote: His worry is **local clients** going under, not technology.
He already uses AI **now and then** and sees it as a small time-saver.
**Rent rises** without pay rises shape his mood more than anything on the card.

steps.text: Keep using the image tool for quick packaging mock-ups
Ask for a January pay review based on the brewery account
Save towards a two-month buffer over the next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who should pay for this are the big platforms, not the cheese farmers and not the designers. I'd back any rule that makes them pay artists whose work trained the tools. At work I'd say we adapt, because we have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I reckon the agency halves. The writing, the social posts, the first drafts of labels, that's all thinking work and it goes first. What's left is the fiddly print side, getting colours and dielines right, and that's me, so I might survive while others don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend evenings getting properly good with the tools, the way I got good with the press specs. I'd go to the boss and propose we sell a packaging-to-print service, where software does drafts and I make sure it actually prints. I'd also join the regional designers' network that's talking about a union, because I'd want company if the agency shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not lost. There's a gap between what the machine draws and what a printer can actually run, and I live in that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said others might not survive. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bella, our copywriter, writes every label's little story about the farm and the cows. That's exactly what these tools do in seconds. I'd feel rotten keeping my job while she loses hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the agency did halve, what would your money look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I stayed, the same thin money but with more work piled on. If I went, I'd be gone in three weeks, because there's no other packaging agency within an hour's drive. That's what keeps me up: there's nowhere else to walk to.

say: I'd say the **big platforms** should pay, not farmers or designers.
At work I'd say we **adapt** because we have to.
think: I reckon the **agency halves** as drafts and copy move to software.
My **print know-how** might keep me there while colleagues go.
do: Spend **evenings learning** the tools properly, like he learned press specs.
Propose a **packaging-to-print** service where he checks software drafts.
Join the regional designers' **network** that's discussing a union.
feel: **Nervous but not lost**, because he knows a gap the machines can't fill yet.
S1.quote: There's a gap between what the machine draws and what a printer can actually run, and I live in that gap.
fieldNote: He blames **big platforms** and wants rules, but plans to adapt pragmatically.
He feels **guilt** about the copywriter whose work goes first.
**No local alternatives** turn a possible layoff into a real threat.

steps.text: Spend two evenings a week learning design AI tools properly
Pitch the boss a packaging-to-print checking service
Join the regional designers' network discussing a union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice somebody made, not the weather. I'd be loud online about a jobs guarantee and a tax on the companies selling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and my design work is gone. The print side buys me a little, maybe until the robots reach the printing floor around 2031, but nobody needs me to check a dieline if the AI does it perfectly. I'd be twenty-nine and starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the brewery for any job they've got, because brewing is hands-on and gets those three extra years. I'd cut everything: no car, no gym, cooking from the market. And I'd sign up for whatever retraining money the government puts up, without any shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like my stomach drops every time I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Idris, sharing the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Idris we've got two years to work out who covers rent if I'm out of work. My cousin Idris is a care worker, so his job lasts longer than mine, and I'm the one with the master's degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stay, because my mum's here. But if the brewery says no and the only work is in the city, I'd go. Two years doesn't give you room to be sentimental.

say: I'd say this is **a choice** somebody made, not the weather.
I'd campaign online for a **jobs guarantee** and a tax on AI firms.
think: My **design work** is gone in two years, and print checking barely buys time.
At **twenty-nine** I'd be starting again from nothing.
do: Ask the **brewery** for hands-on work before the date arrives.
Sell the **car** and cut the gym to stretch the money.
Apply for **government retraining** money as soon as it opens.
feel: **Scared**, with his stomach dropping every time he pictures it.
S2.quote: My cousin Idris is a care worker, so his job lasts longer than mine, and I'm the one with the master's degree.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year robot gap** as useful only if he moves into hands-on work.
The flat share makes it a **household problem**, shared with his cousin.
He'd move for work despite wanting to stay near **his mum**.

steps.text: Ask the brewery for any hands-on brewing job
Sell the car and cancel the gym membership
Apply for government retraining money when it opens
Campaign online for a jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it properly if governments stop sleeping. I'd want design schools telling students the truth now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends my design work, just in 2031. But five years is enough to learn a second thing while I'm still being paid for the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in food production, or brewing, because I already know half the brewery people and it's hands-on. I'd stay at the agency and use the tools daily to keep my value up while it lasts. And I'd get my savings to two months by cutting takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but busy. Busy is better than worried and stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why food and brewing rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've spent five years designing their labels and I actually like those people. The brewer showed me the whole process for a can design once. I'd rather make the beer than draw the can for a machine that doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of design you'd try to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe as a side thing, doing labels for friends who want something made by a person. Like hand-thrown mugs, people pay a bit more for the human version. But I wouldn't bet the rent on it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if governments stop sleeping.
I'd want design schools telling **students the truth** now.
think: My **design work** still ends, just in 2031.
Five years lets me **learn a second thing** while still being paid.
do: Start an **evening course** in brewing or food production.
Use AI tools **daily** at the agency to keep his value up.
Get savings to **two months** by cutting takeaways.
feel: **Worried but busy**, which he prefers to worried and stuck.
S3.quote: I'd rather make the beer than draw the can for a machine that doesn't need me.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose his design job**, but plans a hands-on second trade.
His **client relationships** point him towards brewing.
He'd keep design only as a small **human-made** side line.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening brewing and food production course
Use design AI tools every day at the agency
Cut takeaways to reach two months of savings
Offer hand-made labels to friends as a side line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to build something fair. I'd want a proper public plan for retraining, paid for by the companies that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career's worth of time at my age. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to be good at something new. I might even stay in design for most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency for at least five years, learning the tools and earning. I'd help set up a small co-op with the brewery and the cheese farm to share a designer and a print buyer, which spreads the risk. And I'd save steadily, aiming for three months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Ten years is enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about starting a family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I meet the right person. I'd want to know my income's stable first. A decade is long enough for a kid to arrive before the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the co-op idea. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because small businesses here can't each afford a designer, but together they can. A co-op means the local makers own the tools instead of renting them from a giant. That's my politics and my job in one sentence.

say: I'd say a decade is **time to build** something fair.
I'd want a **public retraining plan** paid for by the companies that profit.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd still be young enough to master something new.
I might **stay in design** for most of the decade.
do: Stay at the agency for **five years**, learning the tools and earning.
Set up a **makers' co-op** sharing a designer with the brewery and cheese farm.
feel: **Uneasy, not scared**, because ten years is enough to plan.
S4.quote: A co-op means the local makers own the tools instead of renting them from a giant.
fieldNote: The decade lets his **politics and job** meet in a co-op idea.
He still expects design to shrink, so his income **could go**, but he feels in control.

steps.text: Stay at the agency and learn the tools for five years
Set up a local makers' co-op sharing one designer
Save steadily towards three months by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years with no savings and no other agencies nearby. What would help is a government that pays for retraining while you're doing it, and rules that make the big platforms share what they earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the small businesses. When my clients go, I go. Nobody talks about the cheese farm when they talk about AI.

headlineQuote: Nobody talks about the cheese farm when they talk about AI.
portrait: Jamal is a **packaging designer** at a six-person harbour agency, working for tiny food businesses and a brewery.
He shares a flat with his **cousin Idris**, earns below city rates and has about two weeks saved.
He uses AI **now and then**, and believes his print know-how gives him a narrow edge.
In fast pictures he'd turn to **brewing**, hands-on work that buys three extra years.
With a decade, he dreams of a **makers' co-op** that owns its tools.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most: no savings and no other agencies within an hour.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while he learns, and rules making big platforms **share earnings**.
